fanoutqa_038407.t: Arabian Desert :: Flora and fauna :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_038407.x:
Arabian Desert :: Flora and fauna :: chunk_0003
The Arabian Desert ecoregion has about 900 species of plants.[[8]](#cite_note-atlas-8) The Rub'al-Khali has very limited floristic [diversity](/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity"). There are only 37 plant species, 20 recorded in the main body of the sands and 17 around the outer margins. Of these 37 species, one or two are endemic. Vegetation is very diffuse but fairly evenly distributed, with some interruptions of near sterile dunes.[[2]](#cite_note-wwf-2) Some typical plants are *[Calligonum crinitum](/w/index.php?title=Calligonum_crinitum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Calligonum crinitum (page does not exist)")* on dune slopes, *[Cornulaca arabica](/w/index.php?title=Cornulaca_arabica&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cornulaca arabica (page does not exist)")* (saltbush), *[Salsola stocksii](/wiki/Salsola_stocksii "Salsola stocksii")* (saltbush), and *[Cyperus conglomeratus](/wiki/Cyperus_conglomeratus "Cyperus conglomeratus")*. Other widespread species are *[Dipterygium glaucum](/w/index.php?title=Dipterygium_glaucum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Dipterygium glaucum (page does not exist)"), [Limeum arabicum](/w/index.php?title=Limeum_arabicum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Limeum arabicum (page does not exist)")*, and *[Zygophyllum mandavillei](/w/index.php?title=Zygophyllum_mandavillei&action=edit&redlink=1 "Zygophyllum mandavillei (page does not exist)")*.
Very few trees are found except at the outer margin (typically *[Acacia ehrenbergiana](/wiki/Acacia_ehrenbergiana "Acacia ehrenbergiana")* and *[Prosopis cineraria](/wiki/Prosopis_cineraria "Prosopis cineraria")*). Other species are a woody perennial *[Calligonum comosum](/wiki/Calligonum_comosum "Calligonum comosum")*, and annual herbs such as *[Danthonia forskallii](/w/index.php?title=Danthonia_forskallii&action=edit&redlink=1 "Danthonia forskallii (page does not exist)")*.[[2]](#cite_note-wwf-2)

Mount Everest :: Expeditions :: 1970s :: chunk_0022
See also: [1970 Mount Everest disaster](/wiki/1970_Mount_Everest_disaster "1970 Mount Everest disaster")

In 1970, Japanese mountaineers conducted a major expedition. The centrepiece was a large "siege"-style expedition, working on finding a new route up the Southwest Face.[[119]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnsworth2000594-127) Another element was an attempt to ski Everest.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) Despite a staff of over one hundred and a decade of planning, the expedition suffered eight deaths and failed to summit.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) However, Japanese expeditions enjoyed some successes. [Yuichiro Miura](/wiki/Yuichiro_Miura "Yuichiro Miura") became the first man to ski down Everest from the South Col—he descended nearly 1,300 vertical metres (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with extreme injuries. Another success was an expedition that put four on the summit via the South Col route.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105)[[120]](#cite_note-128)[[121]](#cite_note-129) Miura's exploits became the subject of film, and he went on to become the oldest person to summit Everest in 2003 aged 70 and in 2013 aged 80.[[122]](#cite_note-130)

In 1975, [Junko Tabei](/wiki/Junko_Tabei "Junko Tabei") became the first woman to summit Everest.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) The [1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition](/wiki/1975_British_Mount_Everest_Southwest_Face_expedition "1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition") led and organised by [Chris Bonington](/wiki/Chris_Bonington "Chris Bonington") made the first ascent of the Southwest Face from the [Western Cwm](/wiki/Western_Cwm "Western Cwm"). In 1978, [Reinhold Messner](/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") and [Peter Habeler](/wiki/Peter_Habeler "Peter Habeler") made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen.

The university is widely considered the birthplace of the computer; mathematician and father of the computer [Charles Babbage](/wiki/Charles_Babbage "Charles Babbage") designed the world's first computing system as early as the mid-1800s. Cambridge alumnus [Alan Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing") devised the basis for modern computing, and [Maurice Wilkes](/wiki/Maurice_Wilkes "Maurice Wilkes") later created the first programmable computer. The [webcam](/wiki/Webcam "Webcam") was also invented at the University of Cambridge, showing the [Trojan Room coffee pot](/wiki/Trojan_Room_coffee_pot "Trojan Room coffee pot") in the university's computer laboratories.

In physics, [Ernest Rutherford](/wiki/Ernest_Rutherford "Ernest Rutherford"), regarded as the father of [nuclear physics](/wiki/Nuclear_physics "Nuclear physics"), spent much of his life at the university, where he worked closely with [E. fanoutqa_011783.x:
Lionel Messi :: Youth career :: Barcelona :: part 01 :: chunk_0007
As the Messi family had relatives in Catalonia, they sought to arrange a trial with [Barcelona](/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") in September 2000, when Messi was 13. First-team director [Carles Rexach](/wiki/Carles_Rexach "Carles Rexach") immediately wanted to sign him, but the board of directors hesitated; at the time it was highly unusual for European clubs to sign foreign players of such a young age. On 14 December, an ultimatum was issued for Barcelona to prove their commitment, and Rexach, with no other paper at hand, wrote a contract on a paper napkin.[[39]](#cite_note-Mission-45)[[42]](#cite_note-Serviette-48) In February 2001, Messi's family relocated to Barcelona, where they moved into an apartment near the club's stadium, [Camp Nou](/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou").[[42]](#cite_note-Serviette-48)

During his first year in Spain, Messi rarely played with the *Infantiles* due to a transfer conflict with Newell's; as a foreigner, he could only be fielded in friendlies and the Catalan league. Without football, he struggled to integrate into the team. He was reserved by nature, and was so quiet that some of his teammates initially believed he was mute. At home, he suffered from homesickness after his mother moved back to Rosario with his brothers and younger sister, María Sol, while he stayed in Barcelona with his father.[[C]](#cite_note-50)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/La_Masia_%28Can_Planas%29_%28Barcelona%29_-_1.jpg/250px-La_Masia_%28Can_Planas%29_%28Barcelona%29_-_1.jpg)](/wiki/File:La_Masia_(Can_Planas)_(Barcelona)_-_1.jpg)

At age 13, Messi enrolled at Barcelona's youth academy, [La Masia](/wiki/La_Masia "La Masia").

Salamanca draws undergraduate and graduate students from across Spain and the world; it is the top-ranked university in Spain based on the number of students coming from other [regions](/wiki/Comunidad_autonoma "Comunidad autonoma").[[19]](#cite_note-19) It is also known for its Spanish courses for non-native speakers, which attract more than two thousand foreign students each year.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Scientific research is carried out in the university and research centers associated with it, such as at the Centro de Investigación del Cáncer [Cancer Research Centre],[[21]](#cite_note-21) Instituto de Neurociencias de Castilla y León or INCyL [Institute of Neuroscience of Castile and León],[[22]](#cite_note-22) Centro de Láseres Pulsados Ultracortos Ultraintensos [Ultrashort Ultraintense Pulse Lasers Centre]. It is one of only two [Hispanophone](/wiki/Hispanophone "Hispanophone") universities in the world that have a [MoU](/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding "Memorandum of understanding") with the [United Nations](/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") to train language professionals for the organization.[[23]](#cite_note-23) In conjunction with the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), the University of Salamanca co-founded the [Association of Language Testers in Europe](/wiki/Association_of_Language_Testers_in_Europe "Association of Language Testers in Europe") (ALTE) in 1989.

In 2018, the institution celebrated its eighth centennial.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

The library holds about 906,000 volumes.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

The **France national football team** ([French](/wiki/French_language "French language"): *Équipe de France de football*) represents [France](/wiki/France "France") in men's international [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football"). It is controlled by the [French Football Federation](/wiki/French_Football_Federation "French Football Federation") (FFF; *Fédération française de football*), the governing body for [football in France](/wiki/Football_in_France "Football in France"). It is a member of [UEFA](/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") in Europe and [FIFA](/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") in global competitions. The team's colours and imagery reference two national symbols: the French [blue-white-red tricolour](/wiki/Flag_of_France "Flag of France") and [Gallic rooster](/wiki/Gallic_rooster "Gallic rooster") (*coq gaulois*). The team is colloquially known as *Les Bleus* (The Blues). They play home matches at the [Stade de France](/wiki/Stade_de_France "Stade de France") in [Saint-Denis](/wiki/Saint-Denis,_Seine-Saint-Denis "Saint-Denis, Seine-Saint-Denis") and train at [Centre National du Football](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_national_du_football "fr:Centre national du football") in [Clairefontaine-en-Yvelines](/wiki/Clairefontaine-en-Yvelines "Clairefontaine-en-Yvelines").

Founded in 1904, the team has won two [FIFA World Cups](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup"), two [UEFA European Championships](/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship "UEFA European Championship"), one [CONMEBOL–UEFA Cup of Champions](/wiki/CONMEBOL%E2%80%93UEFA_Cup_of_Champions "CONMEBOL–UEFA Cup of Champions"), two [FIFA Confederations Cups](/wiki/FIFA_Confederations_Cup "FIFA Confederations Cup") and one [UEFA Nations League](/wiki/UEFA_Nations_League "UEFA Nations League") title.[[3]](#cite_note-3) France was one of the four European teams that participated in the first World Cup in [1930](/wiki/1930_FIFA_World_Cup "1930 FIFA World Cup"). Saint-Exupéry met [Léon Werth](/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Werth "Léon Werth") (1878–1955), a writer and art critic, in 1931. Werth soon became Saint-Exupery's closest friend outside of his [Aeropostale](/wiki/A%C3%A9ropostale_(aviation) "Aéropostale (aviation)") associates. Werth was an anarchist, a leftist [Bolshevik](/wiki/Bolshevik "Bolshevik") supporter [of Jewish descent](/wiki/Jew "Jew"), twenty-two years older than Saint-Exupéry.

Saint-Exupéry dedicated two books to him, *[Lettre à un otage](/w/index.php?title=Lettre_%C3%A0_un_otage&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lettre à un otage (page does not exist)")* (*Letter to a Hostage*) and *Le Petit Prince* (*The Little Prince*), and referred to Werth in three more of his works. At the beginning of the Second World War while writing *The Little Prince*, Saint-Exupéry lived in his downtown New York City apartment, thinking of his native France and his friends. Werth spent the war unobtrusively in [Saint-Amour](/wiki/Saint-Amour,_Jura "Saint-Amour, Jura"), his village in the [Jura](/wiki/Jura_(department) "Jura (department)"), a mountainous region near Switzerland where he was "alone, cold and hungry", a place that had few polite words for French refugees. Werth appears in the preamble to the novella, where Saint-Exupéry dedicates the book to him:[[65]](#cite_note-Saint-Exupéry.a-71)

> To Leon Werth
>
> I ask children to forgive me for dedicating this book to a grown-up. I have a serious excuse: this grown-up is the best friend I have in the world. > To Leon Werth,
>

Djokovic began playing tennis at the age of four,[[8]](#cite_note-biography-9) after his parents gave him a mini-racket and a soft foam ball, which his father said became "the most beloved toy in his life".[[9]](#cite_note-cutler-2016-10) His parents then sent him to a tennis camp in [Novi Sad](/wiki/Novi_Sad "Novi Sad").[[9]](#cite_note-cutler-2016-10) In the summer of 1993, as a six-year-old, he met [Jelena Genčić](/wiki/Jelena_Gen%C4%8Di%C4%87 "Jelena Genčić") at a tennis camp she was overseeing at [Mount Kopaonik](/wiki/Kopaonik "Kopaonik"),[[10]](#cite_note-:1-11): 21–26 where Djokovic's parents ran a fast-food parlour.[[9]](#cite_note-cutler-2016-10)[[11]](#cite_note-spiegel-12)[[12]](#cite_note-NYTimesintro-13) Genčić worked with Djokovic over the following six years, convincing him to hit his backhand with two hands instead of the single hand used by his idol, [Pete Sampras](/wiki/Pete_Sampras "Pete Sampras").[[13]](#cite_note-making1-14)[[14]](#cite_note-nytimes-15) Djokovic has credited Genčić for "shaping my mind as a human being, but also as a professional".[[15]](#cite_note-ausopen-16)[[16]](#cite_note-reuters-17)

Main article: [Volcanoes of Indonesia](/wiki/Volcanoes_of_Indonesia "Volcanoes of Indonesia")

Most of the larger islands are mountainous, with peaks ranging between 2,000 and 3,800 metres (6,562 and 12,467 ft) meters above sea level in Sumatra, Java, Bali, Lombok, Sulawesi, and Seram.[[23]](#cite_note-23) The country's tallest mountains are located in the [Jayawijaya Mountains](/wiki/Jayawijaya_Mountains "Jayawijaya Mountains") and the [Sudirman Range](/wiki/Sudirman_Range "Sudirman Range") in Papua. The highest peak, [Puncak Jaya](/wiki/Puncak_Jaya "Puncak Jaya") (4,884 metres (16,024 ft)), is located in the Sudirman Mountains. A string of volcanoes stretches from Sumatra to Nusa Tenggara,[[24]](#cite_note-24) then loops around through to the [Banda Islands](/wiki/Banda_Islands "Banda Islands") of Maluku to northeastern Sulawesi. Of the 400 volcanoes, approximately 150 are active.[[25]](#cite_note-gvp-25) Two of the most violent volcanic eruptions in modern times occurred in Indonesia; in 1815, [Mount Tambora](/wiki/Mount_Tambora "Mount Tambora") in [Sumbawa](/wiki/Sumbawa "Sumbawa") erupted, killing 92,000, and in 1883, [Krakatau](/wiki/Krakatau "Krakatau") erupted, killing 36,000. While volcanic ashes resulted from eruption has positive effects for the fertility of the surrounding soils, it also makes agricultural conditions unpredictable in some areas.

Further information: [List of Pittsburgh Steelers seasons](/wiki/List_of_Pittsburgh_Steelers_seasons "List of Pittsburgh Steelers seasons")

Through the end of the [2023 season](/wiki/2023_Pittsburgh_Steelers_season "2023 Pittsburgh Steelers season"), the Steelers have an all-time record of 707–606–22, including playoffs. In recent seasons the Steelers have generally performed well, qualifying for the playoffs six times in the past ten seasons, while winning their division four times.[[96]](#cite_note-FranchiseEncyclopedia-96)

In the NFL's "modern era" (since the AFL–NFL merger in 1970) the Steelers have posted the best record in the league. The franchise has won the most regular-season games, the most playoff games (33 playoff wins; the Dallas Cowboys are second with 32), won the most divisional titles (20), has played in the most conference championship games (15), hosted the most conference championship games (11), and is tied with the Dallas Cowboys, the Denver Broncos and the New England Patriots for the most Super Bowl appearances (8).[[97]](#cite_note-x423-97) The Steelers have the best winning percentage (including every expansion team), earned the most All-Pro nominations, and have accumulated the most Super Bowl wins (6) since the modern game started in 1970. In 2017, they became the first team to reach 450 victories in the regular season since the 1970 merger.[[98]](#cite_note-450Wins-98)[[99]](#cite_note-99) The Steelers are 36–26 (.580) in the postseason, with all but one (the 1947 playoff) having been played since the merger.[[100]](#cite_note-100)

fanoutqa_032007.x:
West Coast of the United States :: Definition :: chunk_0001
There are conflicting definitions of which states comprise the West Coast of the United States, but the West Coast always includes [California](/wiki/California "California"), [Oregon](/wiki/Oregon "Oregon"), and [Washington](/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)") as part of that definition. Under most circumstances, however, the term encompasses the three contiguous states and [Alaska](/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), as they are all located in North America. For census purposes, [Hawaii](/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") is part of the West Coast, along with the other four states.[[3]](#cite_note-World_Atlas_definition-4) *[Encyclopædia Britannica](/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica")* refers to the North American region as part of the Pacific Coast, including Alaska and [British Columbia](/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"). Although the encyclopedia acknowledges the inclusion of Hawaii in some capacity as part of the region, the editors wrote that "it has little in common geologically with the mainland states."[[4]](#cite_note-Encyclopædia_Britannica_article-5)

Several dictionaries offer different definitions of the West Coast. [Lexico](/wiki/Lexico "Lexico") restricts the West Coast's definition to "the western seaboard of the U.S. from Washington to California."[[5]](#cite_note-Lexico_definition-6) However, [Macmillan Dictionary](/wiki/Macmillan_Dictionary "Macmillan Dictionary") provides a less specific definition as "the western coast of the U.S., along the [Pacific Ocean](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean")."[[6]](#cite_note-Macmillan_definition-7) As for the [Cambridge Dictionary](/wiki/Cambridge_Advanced_Learner%27s_Dictionary "Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary"), the West Coast is "the area of the Pacific coast in the U.S. that includes California."[[7]](#cite_note-Cambridge_definition-8)
